issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may not reverse concurrent findings of fact merely because it prefers a different view of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both found that the sons had been separated and the Will had been proved.
The High Court reversed those concurrent findings after reassessing the evidence, without identifying an error of law or procedure.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact, and its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 41 of the Punjab Courts Act, 1918, interference with factual findings in a second appeal is confined to errors of law or procedure, not merely errors of fact, however serious they may appear. Pankajakshi (D) through LRs v. Chandrika and Randhir Kaur v. Prithvi Pal Singh were relied on; the latter states that a different preferred view of the facts does not permit interference.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter is a second appeal in which a higher court reviews a lower court's decision.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same findings of fact.
predicates.no_error_of_law_or_procedure: The reviewing court identifies no error of law or procedure underlying the factual findings.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns concurrent factual findings and no error of law or procedure is identified, those findings are left undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a lost document may be considered when a party lays a sufficient foundation for its loss, even without filing a separate application for permission to adduce it.
material_facts: The defendants stated that the original Will, which had been in a beneficiary's possession, was lost.
They produced a certified copy from the Sub-Registrar and a photocopy of the Will; the plaintiff had admitted execution but alleged fraud and misrepresentation.
The defendants' witnesses were not cross-examined about the loss of the original, and no application to lead secondary evidence had been filed.
issues.conclusion: The evidence laid a sufficient foundation for secondary evidence, and it could not be excluded merely because the defendants had not filed a separate application.
issues.legal_principle: Section 65(c) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 permits secondary evidence when an original has been lost. The Court relied on M. Ehtisham Ali v. Jamna Prasad and Aher Rama Gova v. State of Gujarat on proof of loss and admission of secondary evidence, and held that a separate application is not required if the foundation is laid in the pleadings or evidence. Bipin Shantilal Panchal v. State of Gujarat was also relied on regarding the handling of evidentiary objections.

predicates.documentary_proof_proceeding: A party seeks to prove a document in a civil or other evidentiary proceeding.
predicates.original_document_lost: The party offering the document states that the original has been lost.
predicates.secondary_evidence_foundation_laid: The party presents evidence supporting the loss and produces secondary material relating to the document.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to prove a document, the original is stated to be lost, and evidence supports that loss while secondary material is produced, that material may be received without a separate application.

issues.legal_issue: A Will's execution is proved by examining an attesting witness whose evidence establishes the testator's and both attesting witnesses' signatures in the required circumstances.
material_facts: One attesting witness testified that the testator executed the Will and that the witness and the other attesting witness signed it.
The witness stated that the testator also signed the Will at the Tehsil office and that both witnesses witnessed it before the Sub-Registrar.
The witness's evidence that the testator and the other attesting witness were present and signed was not disputed in cross-examination; the scribe and a registration official also gave evidence.
issues.conclusion: The attesting witness's testimony proved due execution of the Will, satisfying the applicable requirements for execution and proof.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 prescribes the formalities for execution and attestation of a Will, and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires at least one attesting witness to be called to prove execution when available. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Seth Beni Chand v. Smt. Kamla Kunwar, and Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam. It distinguished M.L. Abdul Jabbar Sahib v. M.V. Venkata Sastri & Sons and N. Kamalam v. Ayyasamy because the witness examined here was an attesting witness, not merely a scribe.

predicates.will_execution_proof_proceeding: A party seeks to prove the execution of a Will in a court proceeding.
predicates.one_attesting_witness_examined: At least one person who attested the Will gives evidence in the proceeding.
predicates.witness_testifies_testator_and_both_witn: The attesting witness testifies that the testator and both attesting witnesses signed the Will in the required circumstances.

issues.definition: In a proceeding to prove a Will, testimony from one attesting witness establishing the testator's and both witnesses' signatures proves due execution.

issues.legal_issue: The exclusion or omission of natural heirs from a Will does not, by itself, establish a suspicious circumstance invalidating the Will.
material_facts: The Will did not mention the testator's wife or one of his sons.
The High Court treated that omission as a suspicious circumstance, while the defendants relied on evidence that the testator had separated his sons and settled his daughters during his lifetime.
issues.conclusion: The omission of natural heirs was not, by itself, a sufficient reason to treat the Will as suspicious; suspicious circumstances must be assessed cumulatively.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee, which explains that excluding natural heirs is inherent in the purpose of a Will and is not by itself suspicious, and Ved Mitra Verma v. Dharam Deo Verma, which likewise holds that exclusion of children alone is insufficient. Under Leela Rajagopal v. Kamala Menon Cocharan, the court must assess the cumulative effect of unusual features and surrounding circumstances rather than rely on a single feature.

predicates.will_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity or genuineness of a Will.
predicates.will_omits_natural_heirs: The Will excludes or does not mention one or more persons who would otherwise be natural heirs.

issues.definition: When a Will is challenged and omits natural heirs, that omission alone does not establish suspicion about the Will.
